statement_nl: The Ramsey number R(5,5) is the smallest n such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic K_5. It is known that 43 <= R(5,5) <= 46: the lower bound comes from Exoo's 1989 42-vertex counterexample (656 such graphs are known, none extendable to 43 vertices), and the upper bound is a 2024 result (Angeltveit & McKay, arXiv:2409.15709, cited in this repo) obtained after ~80 CPU-years of SAT-based search that tightened the prior bound of 48. The exact value remains unknown.
known_cases: R(4,4)=18 and R(4,5)=25 are known exactly; R(5,5) is the smallest completely open diagonal Ramsey number.
prior_attempts: Extremely heavy prior search: McKay/Radziszowski/Exoo 1997 exhaustive classification of all 656 (5,5,42)-graphs; Angeltveit-McKay 2024 spent ~80 CPU-years of SAT solving to move the upper bound from 48 to 46; multiple GNN/RL agent projects in this same cluster (AutoRamsey, RamseyTheoryRL) have run dedicated search loops against exactly this target with no 43-vertex witness found. This is the single most heavily mined target in the whole cluster.
notes: Improving the LOWER bound by one means exhibiting a single (5,5,43)-graph: a graph on 43 vertices with no 5-clique and no 5-independent-set. Written as an upper-triangular adjacency matrix that is C(43,2) = 903 bits. Verifying a candidate is poly-time (check all C(43,5)=962598 five-subsets for monochromaticity, i.e. no K5 and no I5 -- trivial for a modern machine, well under a second). Note: the AutoRamsey repo in this same cache reports a Lovasz-theta spectral argument suggesting 43-vertex graphs may not exist at all (a 'no' signal, not a construction) -- see mine/cache/h4_LinXueyuanStdio_AutoRamsey/README.md.

statement_nl: The Ramsey number R(4,6) is the smallest n such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic K_4 or a monochromatic independent set of size 6. The repo's reference table gives the current range as 36 <= R(4,6) <= 40.
known_cases: R(4,4)=18, R(4,5)=25 known exactly; R(4,6) open.
prior_attempts: Named as an active target in the RamseyTheoryRL project (mine/cache/h4_aLehav_RamseyTheoryRL) alongside R(5,5); also flagged in arthaschan/r55research's DIRECTION-13-RESEARCH-PLAN.md (which quotes a slightly different range, 35 <= R(4,6) <= 41 -- an internal inconsistency across that repo's own docs worth flagging, not resolved here).
notes: Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a (4,6,36)-graph: 36 vertices, no K4, no independent set of size 6. Adjacency data is C(36,2) = 630 bits. Verification is poly (check all C(36,4) 4-subsets for cliques and C(36,6) 6-subsets for independent sets -- a few million subsets, fast).

statement_nl: The Ramsey number R(5,6) is the smallest n such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic K_5 or a monochromatic independent set of size 6. The repo's reference table gives 59 <= R(5,6) <= 85.
known_cases: Off-diagonal case with R(4,6) and R(5,5) as easier neighbours; not itself a stated focus of the RL/GNN sub-projects in this cluster.
prior_attempts: Not called out as a dedicated machine-search target anywhere in the four cloned repos in this cluster (contrast with R(5,5) and R(4,6)); the 59-85 gap is wide, consistent with less attention.
notes: Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a (5,6,59)-graph: C(59,2) = 1711 bits of adjacency data. Verification poly (check C(59,5) subsets for K5, C(59,6) subsets for I6 -- tens of millions of subsets, still fast to check per-candidate, though the wide 59-85 gap and the size (59 vertices) make blind search much harder than R(4,6).

statement_nl: The Ramsey number R(6,6) is the smallest n such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic K_6. Current range: 102 <= R(6,6) <= 165. The Wikipedia 'Ramsey's theorem' text dump in this cluster's cache (mine/cache/h4_wiki/data/Ramsey's_theorem.txt, line 360) independently corroborates that the R(6,6) lower bound has not been improved since 1965.
known_cases: Far larger gap than R(5,5); the repo's own table (line 51 of the same file) annotates this row '完全无望' (completely hopeless) for the search techniques it uses.
prior_attempts: Lower bound unimproved since 1965 per Wikipedia's Ramsey's theorem article (quoted independently in mine/cache/h4_wiki/data/Ramsey's_theorem.txt line 360: 'lower bounds for r(6, 6) and r(8, 8) have not been improved since 1965 and 1972, respectively'). The authoring repo itself labels this target as hopeless for its GNN-filtered gluing method.
notes: Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a (6,6,102)-graph: C(102,2) = 5151 bits of adjacency data -- an order of magnitude larger search space than R(5,5) (903 bits) and explicitly called out by the source repo as out of reach of its own tooling. Verification is still poly (clique/independent-set check over C(102,6) subsets) but the construction problem is far harder than R(5,5) or R(4,6).

statement_nl: The 4-colour diagonal Ramsey number R(3,3,3,3) is the smallest n such that every 4-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic triangle. Current range: 51 <= R(3,3,3,3) <= 64 (lower bound from a 1970s construction, upper bound from Sanchez-Flores 1995).
known_cases: R(3,3,3)=17 is known exactly (3-colour case); the 4-colour case R(3,3,3,3) is open with a wide gap.
prior_attempts: Lower bound of 51 dates to the 1970s and appears not to have moved since; upper bound of 64 (Sanchez-Flores 1995) is likewise three decades old per the WebSearch summary of Radziszowski's survey lineage -- a long-stale gap, suggesting current SAT/nauty tooling may make faster progress than the historical record implies, or that the problem has resisted exactly such tooling for 30 years.
notes: WebSearch tool's synthesized answer (built from the returned sources) states verbatim: 'For R(3,3,3,3), the upper bound of 64 was established by Sanchez-Flores in 1995 while the lower bound of 51 dates back to the 1970s.' Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a 4-colouring of the edges of K_51 with no monochromatic triangle in any colour: C(51,2)=1275 edges, each needing 2 bits (4 colours) = 2550 bits. Verification is poly (check all C(51,3) triangles for monochromaticity in each of 4 colours).

statement_nl: The 3-colour diagonal Ramsey number R(4,4,4) is the smallest n such that every 3-colouring of the edges of K_n contains a monochromatic K_4. Current range: 128 <= R(4,4,4) <= 229. The lower bound comes from the 127-vertex Hill-Irving graph G_127; the upper bound of 229 is a March-2026 result by Luis Boza.
known_cases: R(4,4)=18 (2-colour case) is known exactly; the 3-colour case has a very wide open gap.
prior_attempts: Boza's paper (arXiv:2603.10851, March 2026) is a very recent upper-bound improvement via a recursive inequality; the lower bound (Hill-Irving's G_127) is decades old and it is reported as still unknown whether G_127 itself even avoids monochromatic triangles under the stated colouring (an open sub-question about the witness itself).
notes: WebSearch synthesis states: 'The 127-vertex graph G127, used by Hill and Irving to prove the bound R(4,4,4) >= 128... The current best upper bound for R(4,4,4) is 229.' Improving the lower bound by one requires a 3-colouring of K_128's edges (C(128,2)=8128 edges) with no monochromatic K4 in any colour: at ~1.585 bits/edge (log2 3) that is roughly 12,880 bits -- an order of magnitude larger than the R(5,5) witness, and the search space (3^8128 colourings) is far beyond brute enumeration; hence witness_check_cost is listed exponential in the worst case although a *given* candidate colouring can still be checked in poly time via clique enumeration -- the exponential cost here is against the raw colouring-space size, not the per-candidate check.

statement_nl: The van der Waerden number W(4,4) is the smallest N such that every 2-colouring of {1,...,N} contains a monochromatic 4-term arithmetic progression. Only a lower bound is known: W(4,4) > 1048 (per a Feb-2023 presentation surfaced by search); no matching finite upper bound short of the generic (very large) van der Waerden-function bound has been established in the sources found.
known_cases: Only 7 van der Waerden numbers are known exactly: W(2,3)=9, W(2,4)=35, W(2,5)=178, W(2,6)=1132, W(3,3)=27, W(3,4)=293, W(4,3)=76. W(4,4) and W(3,5) are not among them.
prior_attempts: Active SAT/computational-search area (multiple 2020-2023 arXiv papers on 'new lower bounds for van der Waerden numbers'); this specific pair is harder than the diagonal W(3,k) cases that have gotten the most attention.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'Regarding lower bounds for W(4,4), the search results show that the lower bound for W(4,4) is greater than 1,048.' No usable upper bound number was returned by search -- recorded as null rather than fabricated, per the harvest rule against inventing figures. Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a 2-colouring of {1,...,1049} (or whatever the current record length is) avoiding monochromatic 4-APs: 1049 bits (1 bit/element for a 2-colouring). Verification is poly (scan all O(N^2) 4-term APs, here ~1.1M, and check colour-monochromaticity of each) -- this is one of the cheapest-to-verify witness types in the whole cluster despite being a hard search target.

statement_nl: The Schur number S(6) is the largest N such that {1,...,N} can be partitioned into 6 sum-free classes (no monochromatic solution to x+y=z with x,y,z not necessarily distinct... i.e. classic Schur, x != y allowed as long as x+y=z is avoided in a single class). Current range: 536 <= S(6) <= 1836, the upper bound following from the Ramsey-number relation S(6) <= R_6(3) - 2.
known_cases: S(1)=1, S(2)=4, S(3)=13, S(4)=44, S(5)=160 (Heule 2017, the famous 200TB 'Schur Number Five' SAT proof) are all known exactly; S(6) is the first open Schur number.
prior_attempts: S(5) required a massive SAT effort (Heule 2017, arXiv:1711.08076, 200TB proof certificate) -- S(6) is the natural next target and is presumably far harder given the 536-1836 gap; a 2022 paper reports S(6) >= 536 as the current record.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'S(6) >= 536 and S(7) >= 1680' plus 'the currently known upper bound is S(6) <= 1836... derived... S(6) <= R_6(3) - 2.' Improving the lower bound by one means exhibiting a partition of {1,...,537} into 6 classes with no monochromatic x+y=z: log2(6)=2.585 bits per element, ~537*2.585 = 1388 bits. Verification is poly (check O(N^2) (x,y) pairs against the colouring, here under 300K pairs).

statement_nl: The weak Schur number WS(6) is the largest N such that {1,...,N} can be partitioned into 6 classes avoiding any monochromatic solution to x+y=z with x < y < z (x=y allowed to be excluded, i.e. the 'weak' variant only forbids the strict-inequality solutions). Only a lower bound is recorded from the sources found: WS(6) >= 646 (a 2022 improvement over an earlier WS(6) >= 582).
known_cases: WS(1)=2, WS(2)=8, WS(3)=23, WS(4)=66 are known exactly; WS(5) and beyond are lower-bound-only.
prior_attempts: Active area: Bouzy's 'Abstract Procedure to Compute Weak Schur Number Lower Bounds' and a 2022 Ageron et al. paper both push this specific record; no matching upper bound appears to be tracked anywhere in the sources found, meaning ANY finite upper bound proof (even a weak one) would itself be a notable partial result, separate from the harder task of raising the lower bound further.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'WS(5) >= 196 and WS(6) >= 582' from one source, refined by 'Improved lower bounds include WS(6) >= 646... established in 2022' from another. Improving the record by one means a 6-colouring of {1,...,647} avoiding weak-Schur triples: ~647*log2(6) = 1673 bits. Verification poly (scan O(N^2) ordered pairs).

statement_nl: z(n;2) (shorthand for the symmetric Zarankiewicz number z(n,n;2,2)) is the maximum number of edges in an n-by-n bipartite graph containing no K_{2,2} (no 4-cycle). Afzaly and McKay computed z(n;2) exactly for all n <= 31; n=32 is the smallest open case, with z(32) known to be either 189 or 190.
known_cases: z(n;2) determined exactly for every n from 1 to 31 (Afzaly-McKay, unpublished per the surfaced source); n=32 is the frontier.
prior_attempts: This is the tightest possible non-trivial gap (upper minus lower = 1) in the whole harvested set -- exhaustive computer search by Afzaly and McKay has already pushed the frontier to exactly this one case, meaning any further progress is either 'find a 190-edge C4-free 32x32 bipartite graph' or 'prove none exists' (both computationally meaningful, bounded tasks).
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'z(32) represents the first open case in the Zarankiewicz problem, and its value is listed as 189/190... Recent unpublished work by Afzaly and McKay pushed the computation of exact Zarankiewicz values z(n;2) to all n <= 31, making z(32) the smallest unsolved case.' Improving the lower bound by one (i.e. exhibiting the 190-edge witness) means producing a 32x32 0/1 biadjacency matrix with no 2x2 all-ones submatrix and exactly 190 ones: naive encoding is 1024 bits (the full matrix), though the true information content is close to log2(C(1024,190)) which is far smaller; either way this is the single cheapest-to-specify, cleanest witness_check_cost=poly target in this whole harvest (check all C(32,2)^2 row/column pairs for a repeated common pair, trivial for nauty/SAT in well under an hour).

statement_nl: cr(K13) is the minimum number of edge crossings over all drawings of the complete graph K13 in the plane. Guy's conjecture predicts cr(K13)=225 (the formula value Z(13)=225). Kleitman's parity theorem restricts cr(K13) to the set {217,219,221,223,225}; successive papers (McQuillan et al.; Abrego et al. 2015) have ruled out 217, 219 and 221, leaving cr(K13) in {223, 225}.
known_cases: cr(K_n) is known exactly (and equals Guy's formula Z(n)) for all n <= 12; K13 is the smallest open case.
prior_attempts: Sustained, incremental progress over at least a decade (McQuillan et al., then Abrego, Fernandez-Merchant et al. 2015) using Kleitman's parity constraint plus ad hoc counting arguments to eliminate candidate values one at a time; this is a textbook case of a family narrowed to a 2-element set by successive exclusion rather than by construction.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'A simple application of Kleitman's parity theorem implies that cr(K13) must be equal to one of the numbers {217, 219, 221, 223, 225}; McQuillan et al. then proved that cr(K13) != 217... Abrego et al. (2015)... showed that cr(K13) != 219 and cr(K13) != 221... narrowed this further: cr(K13) in {223, 225}.' Since cr(K13)=225 is the CONJECTURED (Guy's formula) value, the only way to 'beat the record' here is to exhibit a drawing of K13 with exactly 223 crossings (which would refute Guy's conjecture at n=13) -- a single explicit good drawing, describable as a rotation system (cyclic edge order at each of 13 vertices): roughly 13 * log2(11!) ~= 13*35 ~= 460 bits. Verifying a concrete drawing's crossing count is a direct poly-time combinatorial computation once the drawing is fixed, but confirming REALIZABILITY of an abstract rotation system as an actual plane drawing (not just an abstract combinatorial structure) can require additional planarity-style checks; still practically poly for n=13.

statement_nl: n(3,14) is the number of vertices in the smallest 3-regular (cubic) graph of girth 14 (a (3,14)-cage). The current range is 258 <= n(3,14) <= 384: the lower bound (258, McKay et al. 1998) is a Moore-type counting argument, the upper bound (384, Exoo 2002) is an explicit construction outside the vertex-transitive class, improving on an earlier 406-vertex vertex-transitive example by Hoare (1981).
known_cases: The (3,g)-cages are known exactly for g <= 12 (e.g. (3,11) is the 112-vertex Balaban 11-cage, (3,12) is the 126-vertex Benson graph); g=13 and g=14 remain open, per Exoo & Jajcay's Dynamic Cage Survey.
prior_attempts: A slow-moving 40+ year record: Hoare's 406-vertex construction (1981) stood until Exoo's 384-vertex non-vertex-transitive graph (2002); the lower bound of 258 has stood since McKay et al. 1998. No further published improvement on either side was surfaced by search as of this harvest.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'the lower bound for (3, 14) graphs was improved from 256 to 258 by McKay et al. in 1998. A (3, 14) vertex-transitive graph with order 406 was found by Hoare in 1981, and it was only in 2002 that a smaller (3, 14) graph with order 384 was found by Exoo... current known bounds are: lower bound of 258 and upper bound of 384.' Improving the UPPER bound (the direction where an explicit object helps) means exhibiting a cubic girth-14 graph on fewer than 384 vertices (e.g. 382, since cubic graphs need an even vertex count): as a sparse edge list that's 3*382/2=573 edges, each edge needing about log2(382*381/2)~=16.8 bits => roughly 9600 bits. Verification (confirm 3-regularity and girth >= 14, i.e. no cycle of length <14) is poly via BFS-based girth computation from every vertex -- fast even at this size. Note this is the reverse direction from most entries here: because the LOWER bound for cages comes from counting arguments rather than constructions, an explicit finite object here improves the UPPER bound, not the lower one.

statement_nl: The kissing number K(9) is the maximum number of non-overlapping unit spheres that can simultaneously touch a central unit sphere in 9-dimensional Euclidean space. Henry Cohn's maintained table gives the current range 306 <= K(9) <= 363 (lower bounds from best known lattice/code packings, upper bounds from semidefinite-programming/linear-programming methods).
known_cases: The kissing number is known exactly only in dimensions 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and 24 (the last two via the E8 and Leech lattices, resolved by Musin 2003 and Cohn-Kumar-Miller-Radchenko-Viazovska 2017 respectively). All other dimensions, including this one, are open.
prior_attempts: Kissing number bounds in dimensions 9-24 have been the subject of a long sequence of SDP/LP-bound papers (Bachoc-Vallentin and successors) on the upper side, and explicit lattice/code constructions on the lower side; dimension 9 specifically has not seen a bound tightened to a single value the way dimensions 1-4/8/24 have.
notes: WebSearch synthesis (from Henry Cohn's maintained table, https://cohn.mit.edu/kissing-numbers/ backed by the arXiv source 'TABLE OF KISSING NUMBER BOUNDS HENRY COHN'): 'Dimension 9: Lower bound 306, Upper bound 363'. Improving the lower bound by one requires exhibiting 307 unit vectors in R^9 with pairwise angle >= 60 degrees (equivalently pairwise inner product <= 1/2): 307 vectors of 9 real coordinates each is the raw data; if restricted to a rational/algebraic lattice construction the description is far shorter (just the generating lattice basis, a 9x9 matrix, i.e. 81 numbers) but a from-scratch witness in floating point is 2763 real numbers, not usefully expressed in bits without a precision bound. Verification is poly (compute all pairwise C(307,2) inner products and check the bound) but constructing such a packing is itself a hard continuous optimization problem, not amenable to a SAT/nauty combinatorial search in an hour.

statement_nl: The Turan density pi(K4^(3)) is the supremum edge density of a 3-uniform hypergraph containing no complete 3-graph on 4 vertices (K4 with all 4 triples present). Turan's 1941 conjecture is that pi(K4^(3)) = 5/9 (~0.55556); the best proven upper bound, via Razborov's flag-algebra semidefinite method, is approximately 0.561666. This is a 60+ year open problem in extremal hypergraph theory.
known_cases: The lower-bound construction (a balanced blow-up of a specific 3-coloured triple system on 3 base classes) is well understood and widely believed tight; many non-isomorphic constructions achieving the 5/9 density are known, which is itself cited as evidence the conjecture will be hard to prove (no unique extremal structure to characterize).
prior_attempts: One of the oldest and most heavily studied hypergraph Turan problems; Razborov's flag-algebra machinery (SDP-based, computer-assisted) is the state of the art on the upper-bound side and has not closed the gap despite two decades of refinement since its introduction.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'Turan conjectured the answer is 5/9... Razborov proved that the maximum asymptotic edge density of a 3-uniform hypergraph without a 4-clique is 0.561666... the current best upper bound is approximately 0.561666.' This is an ASYMPTOTIC DENSITY, not a finite-n bound, so it does not fit the finite-object witness template as cleanly as the other entries: improving the lower bound requires a new infinite (or arbitrarily-large-n) construction FAMILY achieving density > 5/9, not a single finite object -- hence witness_type is 'parametric-family' rather than 'finite-object', and per-instance verification of any one such family's asymptotic density is itself a nontrivial (often computer-assisted, flag-algebra-scale) computation, hence witness_check_cost 'exponential'. Not a good target for a 4-core/1-hour nauty+SAT run.

statement_nl: The hat guessing number HG(K_{n,n}) of the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} is the largest number of hat colours for which the players (one per vertex, each seeing all hats except their own along incident edges) have a guaranteed-correct guessing strategy. Gadouleau-Georgiou proved HG(K_{n,n}) <= n+1 in general; Alon et al. showed HG(K_{3,3})=3 is strictly below this bound (the first such example). For K_{4,4} the exact value is open, with 3 <= HG(K_{4,4}) <= 5 (lower bound by monotonicity under the K_{3,3} subgraph, upper bound n+1=5 from the general theorem); a conjecture (unproven) suggests HG(K_{n,n}) <= n for n>=3, which would give HG(K_{4,4}) <= 4.
known_cases: HG(K_{3,3})=3 is the only complete bipartite HG(K_{n,n}) value known to be strictly below the general n+1 upper bound; smaller/simpler graph families (trees, cycles) have HG values known exactly.
prior_attempts: The hat guessing number of graphs is a relatively young (post-2018) but active combinatorics-of-games area (Alon, He, Ido, Przybocki and others); K_{4,4} is explicitly named in the literature as the natural next open case after K_{3,3}, but appears not to have been resolved as of the sources surfaced here.
notes: WebSearch synthesis: 'Gadouleau and Georgiou proved HG(K_{n,n}) <= n+1... HG(K_{3,3})=3, which makes this the first complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} for which the hat-guessing number is known to be smaller than the upper bound of n+1... It remains an interesting open question to determine the value of HG(K_{n,n}) for n>3... known bounds are: 3 <= HG(K_{4,4}) <= 5.' A hat-guessing strategy witness is a family of guessing functions (one per vertex, mapping observed neighbour-colours to a guess) for a claimed number of colours c; for c=4 or 5 colours on 4 vertices the strategy table size is c^{(deg-1)} per vertex-ish, which grows fast -- this is why witness_check_cost is 'exponential' (verifying a full strategy against all c^4 colourings of K_{4,4}'s vertices is a brute-force check over the full colouring space, 4^4=256 or 5^4=625 -- actually small enough here to be practically poly at this tiny size, but the family in general is exponential in n).

statement_nl: A Costas array of order N is an NxN permutation matrix such that all displacement vectors between pairs of 1-entries are distinct (equivalently, no two of the N(N-1)/2 difference vectors between marked cells coincide). It is open whether a Costas array of order 32 (or 33) exists: known algebraic construction methods (Welch, Lempel, Golomb) do not produce arrays for these orders, and no example has been found by exhaustive or heuristic search either, as of the survey found by this harvest.
known_cases: Costas arrays are known to exist for essentially all small N via algebraic constructions except a handful of orders (famously N=32 and N=33) that fall outside the reach of the Welch/Lempel/Golomb families; enumeration efforts (e.g. 'The enumeration of Costas arrays of order 28') have exhaustively resolved smaller orders.
prior_attempts: Exhaustive search for Costas arrays gets combinatorially harder very fast with N (order-28 enumeration alone was a substantial computational project); N=32/33 sit right past the frontier of both algebraic construction theory and brute-force enumeration, per Drakakis's 'Open problems in Costas arrays' survey (arXiv:1102.5727).
notes: This entry does not fit the lower!=upper numeric-bound template as cleanly as the others: it is an EXISTENCE gap, not a value gap. WebSearch synthesis: 'The smallest values of n for which no Costas array of order n is currently known are n=32 and 33... It remains unknown if there exist any Costas arrays of size 32 or 33. Costas arrays are conjectured to exist for all values of n, but several algebraic construction methods cannot build Costas arrays of size 32 and some higher non-prime sizes.' current_bounds.lower is recorded as 0 (zero verified examples known) with upper left null (no nonexistence proof). The witness is a single 32x32 permutation matrix (i.e. a permutation of {1..32}, so 32*log2(32)=160 bits, or more precisely log2(32!)~=117 bits of real information) satisfying the distinct-differences property. Verification is poly: compute all 32*31/2=496 displacement vectors from a candidate permutation and check for a repeat -- trivial, well within a SAT/brute-force search's per-candidate budget; the difficulty is entirely in the SIZE of the search space (32! permutations), not in checking any one candidate.
